rounds.fact: About.com organized the web using human 'guides' who curated links on specific topics, a labor-intensive model for making sense of the internet before search engines got good enough to do it automatically.
Blizzard's late-90s site supported both Diablo and StarCraft, two games that helped define entire genres and whose online play features were unusually ambitious for their time.
Allrecipes built its entire catalog from user-submitted recipes rather than professional chefs, an early example of crowdsourced content outperforming edited, expert-driven sites.
PayPal originally grew by paying users real money just to sign up and refer friends, an aggressive growth tactic that helped it become the dominant way to pay on eBay.
The Drudge Report has used essentially the same barebones, all-links homepage design since the late 90s, a deliberate choice that's stayed almost untouched for over two decades.
